newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Italy's Prodi pledges "new dawn" for Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi pledges "new dawn" for Albania.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Sunday that a multi-national security force could aid the "rebirth" of Albania after weeks of violent unrest.
Prodi, warmly welcomed by thousands of cheering Albanians, said the mission, codenamed "Alba" (dawn) by the Italians, could help Europe's poorest nation restore law and order.
"The mission is called 'Alba'," Prodi said. "And this could be the dawn in the history of Albania, the rebirth of Albania."

Nearly 300 people have been killed and about 700 hurt in an armed uprising over the last six weeks since the collapse of get-rich-quick investment schemes in which many Albanians lost their life savings.
Prodi, at the cost of a rift with his hard left allies, won parliament's approval last week for Italy to spearhead the 6,000-strong multinational force.
Its mission is to safeguard emergency food and medicine supplies. Advance units arrived on Friday and the bulk of the force is due on Tuesday.

Escorted by heavily-armed Italian marines, Prodi arrived in a convoy of three Italian army helicopters in the rebel-held southern port city of Vlore, where he was welcomed by more than 10,000 Albanians.
Prodi met Albania's Prime Minister Bashkim Fino in Vlore, where they discussed the precise role of the Italian-led force.
"We want it to be rapid, efficient and peaceful," Prodi told a news conference. "We do not intend to intervene in domestic Albanian politics."
Prodi also expressed his condolences to the victims of a refugee boat that was sunk off Italy on March 28 after colliding with an Italian naval vessel.
Prodi called for a moment of silence for the victims of Albania's worst maritime disaster. About 60 journalists and local officials at the news conference stood quietly.
Tirana says at least 80 Albanians, mostly from Vlore, were killed and many of the 34 survivors accused the Italians of ramming the boat, charges Italy denied.

Vlore has been a focal point of the recent unrest, with 135 people killed and 537 wounded. Prodi planned to visit last week, but a new outbreak of violence prompted Fino to urge postponement of the meeting.
The Italian leader was due to meet Albania's President Sali Berisha in Tirana later on Sunday.
Although Kalashnikov rifles were visible everywhere in Vlore, security for Prodi was extremely tight and the prime minister received a thunderous welcome from local residents.
Thousands lined the road leading into town and cheered as he rode by in a motorcade of about 30 cars and armoured vehicles.
Banners reading "Welcome Mr Prodi" along with "We Want Our Money Back" were held up by spectators along the road into town.
An estimated 10,000 people jammed a central town square in front of a university building where Prodi and Fino met local leaders in the rebel stronghold.

"It is a privilege to have Prime Minister Prodi here in our city," said Albert Shyti, the leader of the national salvation committee in Vlore. The rebel group took control of the south during the armed uprising earlier this year.
"I do not think there will be any danger to the Italians here," said Shyti, who also welcomed Prodi.
Outside the meeting, the crowd also chanted profanities, in Italian, deriding President Berisha, whom many southern Albanians blame for the chaos sweeping the nation.

Advance Italian troops of the 6,000-strong mission have already arrived to make preparations for the main force, which will also include soldiers from France, Spain, Greece, Turkey, Austria, Denmark and Romania.
Some 3,500 Albanian troops, including commandos and tank brigades, will help the multinational mission, officials said.

The first French troops joining the mission arrived in the western port city of Durres on Sunday. Forty French soldiers from the ship Chamberlain disembarked after sailing across the Adriatic from the Italian port of Brindisi.
